title: ANGPTL3/8 is an atypical unfoldase that regulates intravascular lipolysis by catalyzing unfolding of lipoprotein lipase as measured by hydrogen/deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS)
projectDescription: Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) carries out the lipolytic processing of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins (TRL) along the luminal surface of capillaries. LPL activity is regulated by angiopoietin-like proteins (ANGPTL3, ANGPTL4, and ANGPTL8), which control the delivery of TRL-derived lipid nutrients to tissues in a temporal and spatial fashion. This regulation mediates the partitioning of lipid delivery to storage and metabolic tissues according to nutritional status. A complex between ANGPTL3 and ANGPTL8 (ANGPTL3/8) inhibits LPL activity in oxidative tissues, but its mode-of-action has remained unknown. Here, we used biophysical techniques to define how ANGPTL3/8 and ANGPTL3 interact with LPL and how they drive LPL inactivation. We demonstrate, by mass photometry, that ANGPTL3/8 is a heterotrimer with a 2:1 stoichiometry between ANGPTL3 and ANGPTL8 and that ANGPTL3 is a homotrimer. Hydrogen–deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) studies revealed that both ANGPTL3/8 and ANGPTL3 use the proximal portion of their N-terminal α-helices to interact with sequences surrounding the catalytic pocket in LPL. That binding event triggers unfolding of LPL’s α/β- hydrolase domain and irreversible loss of LPL catalytic activity. The binding of LPL to its endothelial transporter protein (GPIHBP1) or to heparan-sulfate proteoglycans protects LPL from inactivation by unfolding, particularly against the unfolding triggered by ANGPTL3. Pulse-labelling HDX-MS studies revealed that ANGPTL3/8 and ANGPTL3 catalyze LPL unfolding in an ATP-independent fashion, which categorize these LPL inhibitors as atypical unfoldases. The catalytic nature of LPL unfolding by ANGPTL3/8 explains why low plasma concentrations of ANGPTL3/8 are effective in inhibiting a molar excess of LPL in capillaries.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Continuous Labeling. This labeling protocol is used to measure changes in solvent exposure and conformational flexibility in pairs of interacting proteins thus providing molecular insights into binding interfaces and allosteric consequences of their binding. The D2O buffer was 20 mM HEPES, 150 mM NaCl pH 7.6 prepared in deuterium oxide (D, 99.9%) unless stated otherwise. To map binding interfaces on ANGPTL3 and ANGPTL3/8 for LPL, we incubated 0.5 µM ANGPTL3 or ANGPTL3/8 with 1 µM bovine LPL in 20 mM HEPES, 150 mM NaCl pH 7.6 for 5, 25, 50, 100, and 1,000 s in 90% D2O at 25°C before quenching further exchange by adding 1 vol of ice-cold quench buffer (100 mM H2HPO4, 800 mM Tris-(2 carboxyethyl)phosphine, and 2 M urea in H2O, pH 2.5) and incubating on ice for an additional 2 min to reduce disulphide bonds. The samples were snap frozen in liquid N2 and stored at −80°C until further analysis by mass spectrometry. To map the binding site on LPL for ANGPTL3 and ANGPTL3/8, we initially pre-incubated 5 µM bovine LPL with 12 µM GPIHBP1 for 10 min on ice before adding buffer or 7.8 µM ANGPTL3 or ANGPTL3/8 (20 mM HEPES, 150 mM NaCl, pH 7.6) and continuing incubation on ice for 5 min. The protein mixtures were pre-equilibrated for 30 s at 25°C before isotope exchange was initiated by adding 9 vol of D2O buffer at 25°C. Deuterium exchange proceeded for 5, 25, 50, 100, and 1000 s before the reaction was quenched. Maximally labeled controls were prepared by diluting samples in 10 mM HEPES, 150 mM NaCl, 2 M urea-d4 in 90% D2O buffer, pH 7.0 and incubated at 37°C and on a thermoshaker (300 rpm) for 48 h to approach exchange equilibrium. Quenching was conducted as described above except the quench buffer did not contain urea to balance the deuterium content in the final sample. All experiments were performed in triplicates.  Pulse Labeling. We used pulse-labeling to quantify the relative abundances of co-existing LPL conformations i.e., natively folded vs. irreversibly unfolded states. To estimate thermal unfolding of LPL at different temperatures, we incubated 7.5 µM bovine LPL either alone or in the presence of 12 µM GPIHBP1 and/or 5 µM of either ANGPTL3 or ANGPTL3/8 for 180 s in protiated buffer (20 mM HEPES, 150 mM NaCl pH 7.6) at 20°C, 30°C, and 40°C. After a 30 s temperature equilibration at 25°C, the samples were subjected to a 10 s pulse labeling by adding 9 vol of D2O buffer preheated to 25°C.  To assess the unfoldase activity of ANGPTL3 and ANGPTL3/8, we incubated 7.5 µM bovine LPL either alone or in the presence of 12 µM GPIHBP1 and/or 0.8 µM of either ANGPTL3 or ANGPTL3/8 for 5, 10, 25, 50, and 100 s at 37°C in the protiated buffer described above. Samples were temperature equilibrated for 10 s at 25°C before pulse labeling for 10 s by addition of 9 vol D2O buffer preheated to 25°C. Quenching was carried out as described for continuous labeling.  Data acquisition. The quenched samples were injected directly into a sample loop (200 μL) at 0.2°C mounted in a HDX-Manager (Waters Corporation, MA, USA), and digested online by agarose immobilized pepsin (ThermoFisher, MA, USA) at 20°C packed in a 2.0×20 mm column (IDEX Upchurch guard column, WA, USA). The peptic peptides were trapped and desalted by reversed-phase chromatography with a ACQUITY UPLC BEH C18 VanGuard Precolumn (130 Å, 1.7 μm, 2.1×5 mm, Waters). A flow of 0.23% (v/v) aqueous formic acid solution (Solvent A) at 300 μL/min provided by an Agilent 1260 Infinity quaternary pump (Agilent Technologies, CA, USA) was used for on-line digestion as well as to desalt the peptic peptides for a total of 3 min. Subsequently, the peptic peptides were chromatographically separated using a 1.0×50 mm ACQUITY UPLC Peptide BEH C18 Column (300 Å, 1.7 μm, 1.0×50 mm, Waters) at 0.2°C with a gradient flow comprised of Solvent A and Solvent B (0.23% (v/v) formic acid in acetonitrile). The gradient was delivered by a nanoAcquity ultra-performance liquid chromatography (UPLC) Binary Solvent Manager (Waters Corporation, MA, USA). The peptides were eluted with the following gradient, 5–10% B for 0.1 min, 10–50% B for 11.9 min, 50–90% B for 0.5 min, 90%-90% B for 0.1 min and 90-5% B for 0.1 min at 40 μL/min, into the electrospray ionization (ESI) ion source and mass-analyzed with a Synapt G2, quadrupole time-of-flight tri-wave ion mobility mass spectrometer (Waters Corporation, MA, USA). Peptides were identified by data-dependent LC-MS/MS experiments using an Orbitrap Eclipse mass spectrometer (Thermo FisherScientific, San Jose, CA, USA). To ensure identical peptide retention times in the HDX-MS analyses and in the LC-MS/MS identification experiments, the peptides were separated with same chromatographic equipment and methods. The precursor ions were automatically selected for MS/MS from Orbitrap survey MS scans in the mass range of m/z 300 – 1500, and subsequently fragmented by collision-induced dissociation using a normalized collision energy of 30% in a 1 s cycle.
dataProcessingProtocol: Peptide deuterium uptake curves were obtained from DynamX 3.0 (Waters Corporation, MA, USA), and deuterium uptake values were exported from this software. Peptides were identified by data-dependent LC-MS/MS experiments using an Orbitrap Eclipse mass spectrometer (Thermo FisherScientific, San Jose, CA, USA). The resulting raw files were converted to MGF files using ProteoWizard, and the peptides were identified by a Mascot database search with the following parameters: variable modifications (oxidation, M), peptide mass tolerance ±0.1 Da; fragment ion mass tolerance ± 7 ppm; enzyme, none. The Mascot database contained the proteins of interest as well as possible contaminating proteins
